data.Unnamed: 3:
ISCED 24 is organised in two tracks:
•	Compulsory secondary schools (MS – Mittelschulen) leading to a vocational or to a one-year pre-vocational programme at ISCED 34 (PS – Polytechnische Schule). 
•	Academic secondary schools (AHS – Allgemeinbildenden höheren Schulen). This type of school covers both lower and upper secondary education (4 in lower secondary education and 4 in upper secondary education). The curriculum is common until the end of grade 6.

ISCED 24 is organised in two tracks:
•	Compulsory secondary schools (MS – Mittelschulen) leading to a vocational or to a one-year pre-vocational programme at ISCED 34 (PS – Polytechnische Schule). 
•	Academic secondary schools (AHS – Allgemeinbildenden höheren Schulen). This type of school covers both lower and upper secondary education (4 in lower secondary education and 4 in upper secondary education). The curriculum is common until the end of grade 6.

Students who successfully pass the primary education certificate (CEB – certificat d’études de base; 86.07% of students) follow the curriculum described in the data collection. For others, a specific program (1er degré differencié) supports them in completing the certificate. 

The data reflect the minimum number of hours in public institutions; however, the curriculum in government-dependent private institutions is similar.
data.:: At ISCED 1, the reform of the common core curriculum is being gradually implemented between 2022/2023 and 2025/2026. To support differentiation and personalised support practices, additional supervision resources have been provided under the Pact for Excellence in Teaching. They should enable class groups to benefit from a co-teacher for several hours a week.

data.Unnamed: 3:
There are 2 different tracks at ISCED 24:
•	the general A-stream programme described here; 
•	the B-stream programme (16.3% of students) with similar instruction time, except that: a) there is no second foreign language (language 3); b) in grade 8, at least 37.5% are compulsory flexible subjects chosen by schools (instead of 21.9%).

In the Flemish Community of Belgium, around two-thirds of students in primary and secondary education are enrolled in government-dependent private institutions. The main difference with publiic institutions is that, although government-dependent private institutions must provide instruction time in their curricula for religion/ethics/moral education, no minimum number of periods is indicated.

data.:: At ISCED 24, the yearly hours dedicated to ICT have been gradually increased between 2021/2022 and 2023/2024.

data.Unnamed: 3:
Apart from a minimum number of lessons for physical education, no standard curriculum or instruction time is defined nationally. Curricula and planned instruction time are set by the 26 cantons at the regional level. Definitions and numbers of both compulsory and non-compulsory subjects, along with the total instruction time and distribution among subjects, vary significantly across cantons. Therefore, only data on total instruction time per grade and ISCED level can be presented:
•	At ISCED 1, the total compulsory instruction time for the six grades varies between 4 509 hours and 5 189 hours across cantons. 
•	At ISCED 24, the total compulsory instruction time for the three grades varies between 2 602 hours and 3 062 hours.
data.not available:
The figures represent weighted averages of cantonal requirements for each grade and total instruction time as provided in cantonal timetables (Stundentafeln / grilles horaires). The averages are weighted by the number of students per canton at ISCED 1 (six years) and ISCED 24 (three years) in 2022/2023. In Ticino, ISCED 1 was a 5-year programme and ISCED 24 a 4-year programme. However, for the sake of comparability the calculations are based on six years at ISCED 1 and three years at ISCED 24. The instruction time provided for ISCED 24 is the mean of the different tracks (basic and advanced requirements; not including baccalaureate schools in grade 9).

The number of instruction days per school year is presented as an average of the number of school weeks per year (varying between 36.5 and 40 weeks) minus an estimated average of five public holidays. Teacher development days are at the discretion of the school and therefore cannot be excluded.

They are obliged to introduce the following subjects by the grades specified: the first foreign language by the spring term of grade 1; the second foreign language by grade 6; social sciences by grade 4; and home economics, guidance and counselling (practical and vocational skills) by grade 7.
data.:: In 2024/2025, the total number of hours for a second foreign language at ISCED 24 increased by 28 hours.

Two new initiatives in the ISCED 24 curriculum:
•	In grade 6: approximatively 36 yearly hours - usually one hour per week - allocated to the compulsory ‘homework done’ programme (supervised homework decided by the school head) implemented since the beginning of 2023-2024 school year.
•	Gradual implementation of up to 18 yearly hours for student involvement and participation in citizenship, media and information education projects in grades 7 to 9 between 2024/2025 and 2026/2027.

The new National Core Curriculum and the related National Framework Curriculum were gradually implemented since 2020/2021 and applied to all grades since the 2024/2025 school year. The reform aimed at developing key competencies aligned with EU recommendations, such as learning, communication, digital, and entrepreneurial skills, while emphasizing ‘development fields’ such as ethics, national identity, and sustainability. It sought to improve learning effectiveness, reduce student workload, and ensure that the curriculum reflects current pedagogical research and societal values.
data.not available: The data collection is based on the National Framework Curriculum, which is compulsory for all grades.

data.Unnamed: 3: The national curriculum guidelines allocate time for compulsory options. All schools use this time for extra teaching time both for compulsory subjects and for subjects that students may choose.

Schools have autonomy in the distribution of the timetable over the week:
•	At ISCED 1, the reported curriculum corresponds to the three most common types of timetable: 27 weekly hours (28.99% of students); 28-30 hours (27.67% of students); and 40 hours (42,70% of students). A small proportion of students (0.64%) have a weekly timetable of 24 hours, with a different total amount of time and distribution by subject.
•	At ISCED 24, the reported instruction time corresponds to a weekly timetable of 30 hours (84.22% of students). This timetable also applies to students following the music pathway (8.76%), with 99 additional hours per year for the teaching of the musical instrument and music theory. Some students have a different programme with a higher number of hours per week (7.02%).
At all ISCED levels, schools have the autonomy to modify up to 20% of the annual timetable by changing the allocation of instruction time across subjects or by introducing new subjects.
data.:: Between 2023/2024 and 2024/2025, two additional weekly hours of motor education were added to the timetables of all the possible weekly organisations for the last two grades of ISCED 1 (except in the 40-hour organisation).

data.not available: Between September and May, the weekly instruction time correspond to 5.25 hours per day at ISCED 1 education (26.25 weekly hours) and 5.5 hours per day at ISCED 24 (27.5 weekly hours). data.Unnamed: 3:
Three different tracks co-exist, with different durations:
•	Pre-vocational secondary education(VMBO - Voortgezet Middelbaar Beroepsonderwijs) ends after 4 years in secondary education. There are 4 different learning pathways in VMBO: basic vocational programme (VMBO-B); middle-management vocational programme (VMBO-K); combined programme (VMBO-G); and theoretical programme (VMBO-T).
•	Senior general secondary education(HAVO - Hoger algemeen voortgezet onderwijs) prepares student for higher professional education and ends after 5 years in secondary education (3 at ISCED 24; 2 at ISCED 34).
•	Pre-university education(VWO - Voorbereidend wetenschappelijk onderwijs) prepares students for higher professional education and ends after 6 years in secondary education (3 at ISCED 24; 3 at ISCED 34).
data.not available:
For ISCED 1, the top-level recommendation specifies a total compulsory instruction time for basic education (basisonderwijs groep 1-8). This corresponds to the last two grades in pre-primary and the six grades at ISCED 1. It is at the discretion of the individual school to distribute these hours across grades. The calculation for ISCED 1 is based on the prorated number of grades.

National regulations also provide for some vertical flexibility between ISCED 24 and 34 (between grades 7 and 11) in VWO. The instruction time for these cycles was artificially prorated by the number of years concerned per ISCED level. 

For ISCED 24, weighted averages of the instruction time in different tracks are reported (HAVO, VMBO and VWO). As the number of grades in lower secondary education is 3 or 4 years depending on the track, the fourth year of pre-vocational secondary education (VMBO) was excluded from the calculation.

data.Unnamed: 3: At ISCED 1 and ISCED 24, schools may reallocate up to 5% of the total ordinary instruction time for each subject to other curriculum subjects. Subject time can be reallocated only within the same stage, i.e. grades 1-4, 5-7 and 8-10.

School governing bodies, at the request of school heads, may additionally grant up to three hours a week to each class in a given school year to enable a periodic or annual increase in the number of hours of instruction for selected compulsory subjects.

Maximum and minimum instruction times are set for each subject. Each school chooses the time to allocate by subject within the established limits: the minimum amount of time per subject and the total amount of time per year.

Municipalities with an official minority language (Bosnian, Bulgarian, Czech, Montenegrin, Croatian, Hungarian, Macedonian, Romany, Romanian, Rusyn, Slovak, Albanian) can organise classes in this language. Schools in which Serbian is the language of instruction can offer a minority language with national culture elements as a non-compulsory subject, which students from minority populations can choose or not (72 lessons a year).

data.:: The distribution of instruction time has changed between 2022/2023 and 2024/2025, although the total number of instruction hours remains the same. The compulsory options chosen by the students was suppressed (-177 hours), except for the hours dedicated to a second foreign language – usually German, French or Spanish – or sign language, a home language, advanced Swedish or English. Instead, the total number of hours of instruction time increased for some other subjects: social sciences (+95 hours), natural sciences (+50 hours), arts education (+20 hours), and practical and vocational skills (+12 hours).

data.Unnamed: 3: In areas where Italian and Hungarian ethnic minorities live, schools implement adapted curricula, which include two more lessons per week and a slightly different allocation of the instruction time between subjects, as students must learn two languages – Slovenian and Italian or Hungarian. The adapted curriculum is followed by 3.9% of students in public schools. The remaining 1.2% of students follow an adapted curriculum in government-dependent private schools.
data.:: In the 2024/2025 school year, the first foreign language (language 2) has been implemented as compulsory for all schools in grade 1 of ISCED 1.

In 2023, the Ministry of Education approved a new curriculum for primary and lower secondary education. Schools will gradually implement this reform as of 2026/2027, starting with grade 1. Pilot implementation has already begun in selected schools. The changes are part of the curriculum reform which focuses on meeting the 21st century educational needs − critical thinking, digital, and soft skills. The curriculum introduces specific education targets, school leaver profiles, or framework educational plans. The performance and content standards define what students should know at the end of each education cycle, that is at grades 3, 5, and 9 of basic education.

data.Unnamed: 3: Information on the decision-making level refers to universities (Universitäten) and university colleges of teacher education (Pädagogische Hochschulen). Universities of applied sciences (Fachhochschulen/Hochschulen für Angewandte Wissenschaften) and private higher education institutions have institutional autonomy to decide on the start of the academic year (generally in September or October).

The Higher Education Code specifies that the academic year should start between 1 September and 1 October.
No information is available regarding the independent private sector.
No information is available regarding the independent private sector.
Some private universities start the academic year in September.

The Act on Higher Education and Scientific Activity specifies that the academic year spans between 1 October and 30 September of the following year. Under specific circumstances, some courses may start as early as 1 September.
Some private higher education institutions start the academic year in October.
The official start of the academic year is in August, as defined by the top-level authority.

The decision on the start of the academic year is made by the Länder. For universities of applied sciences (Hochschulen für angewandte Wissenschaften/Fachhochschulen), the academic year typically starts in September.

At ISCED 6, the top-level authority sets the official start of the academic year at 1 September, while institutional higher education institutions determine the start of teaching activities. At ISCED 7, the academic year may start in October or March.
In the private sector the academic year usually starts in October.
No information is available regarding the independent private sector.
For private institutions, the start of the academic year happens at different times of the year.
Some higher education institutions will exceptionally start the academic year in November to adjust to the prolongation of the previous academic year (due to socio-political circumstances).

The top-level authority determines the start of the academic year, as well as the dates of autumn and spring semesters. However, the Institutes decide independently on the periods when teaching activities start.

In some autonomous communities, some non-university tertiary programmes start in October. For those, the autonomous community usually decides on the start of the academic year. However, the decision may be delegated to the provincial directorates or the municipalities.
No information is available regarding the independent private sector.

data.System-level indicators for monitoring e: System-level indicators on early leaving from education and training (ELET)
Indicator 1: Early warning systems for preventing ELET, ISCED 1-34, 2024/2025

data.Unnamed: 1: Yes, an early warning system for preventing ELET exists
data.Unnamed: 2: No, an early warning system for preventing ELET does not exist

data.Unnamed: 4: Early warning systems are data-driven tools designed to identify and respond to early signs of student disengagement that may lead to early leaving from education and training (ELET). These signs may include poor school attendance or absenteeism, problematic behaviour, low academic performance, grade repetition, social-emotional difficulties, or contact with social services or law enforcement. In addition to these indicators, early warning systems may also capture students’ sense of well-being and belonging at school, as well as experiences of bullying or discrimination.

Early warning systems support the monitoring of student progress and the sharing of information across educational authorities, institutions, teachers, and parents. At the student level, they provide a comprehensive overview of each learner’s needs in one centralised place, enabling schools - together with relevant pedagogical support services - to plan and implement targeted, preventative interventions.
Bulgaria: The early warning system covers students of compulsory preschool and school age, from 4 to 16 years, i.e. not until the end of ISCED 34.
France: Measures only apply to ISCED 24-34.

Latvia: A Education quality monitoring system, which includes early warning data to decrease early leaving risks is currently being developed (https://www.izm.gov.lv/lv/izglitibas-kvalitates-monitoringa-sistema).
Lithuania: NEMIS system collects data on children and young people up to 16 years, i.e.  ISCED 1-24. Other registers cover ISCED 1-34.

Netherlands: A new law on school absenteeism will be implemented in August 2025, which will ensure better monitoring of attendance and faster targeted actions to prevent ELET (https://wetgevingskalender.overheid.nl/Regeling/WGK014222).

Portugal: An interactive platform is under development, that will allow school heads and school departments to identify students at risk of early school leaving, and to define strategies to address the issue at school level.

Slovakia: A national project has been launched to develop and test an early warning system that identifies school students at risk of ELET and provides targeted support, with full national implementation by 2028/29 (https://www.minedu.sk/ministerstvo-skolstva-spusta-projekt-prevencie-predcasneho-ukoncenia-skolskej-dochadzky/).

Indicator 2: Learners targeted in top-level policies on individual education plans (IEPs), ISCED 1–34, 2024/2025

data.Unnamed: 8: An individual education plan (IEP) is a personalised plan or programme of action that outlines the instruction, adaptations, and support mechanisms to be provided in order to support students’ learning according to their individual targets. It can serve as a valuable tool for delivering more comprehensive and effective support to learners.

IEPs are traditionally developed for students with special educational needs or disabilities. However, extending the use of IEPs to all learners—not only those with special educational needs—can help promote inclusive education by addressing the diverse learning needs of all students.
Belgium (BE fr) and Denmark: Data only apply to ISCED 1 and 24.

Belgium (German-speaking Community): Policy for learners with SEN/disability only applies to ISCED 1. 'Other learners' refers to 12 to 18-year-olds (ISCED 24 and 34) who are disconnected from school or training due to social and emotional issues. The Time Out facility helps them work on projects to build motivation and skills for their future education and career goals.
Bulgaria: 'Other learners' refers to students in an individual form of study (see Policy_description_Indicator_2).

Czechia: In addition to those learners explicitly referred to in the legislation, any other student who needs support measures, including individual education plans, is eligible based on consent from the School Guidance and Counselling facility. 'Other learners' refers to exceptionally gifted pupils (at ISCED 1-34).
Estonia: IEPs are more detailed for ISCED 1-24 than for 34; and with differing graduation conditions depending on whether they apply to basic or upper secondary education.
Spain: 'Other learners' refers to students with late entries into the Spanish educational system.
Croatia, Poland, Slovenia and Serbia: 'Other learners' refers to gifted children and students.

Italy: 'Other learners' refers to students not covered by the laws on students with disabilities or with learning disorders; each class council can autonomously decide if an IEP is necessary for them.
Latvia: 'Other learners' refers to those who have returned from living in other country (reemigrants).

Lithuania: 'Other learners" refers to learners requiring an IEP due to various circumstances like upper secondary education enrolment, returning from abroad, home-schooling on medical advice, studying in specialised or corrective institutions, pursuing simultaneous vocational training, or having special educational needs or exceptional talents.
Austria: At ISCED 34 there are no mandatory IEPs. 'Other learners' refers to students with a lack of knowledge of the language of instruction.

Slovakia: 'Other learners' refers to students whose disabilities, social/economic/family circumstances, language abilities, talents, behaviour, cognitive abilities, motivation, emotionality, creativity, or skills necessitate specific support measures.

Finland: Data only apply to ISCED 1 and 24. 'Other learners' refers to students in the "Preparatory Education for Programmes Leading to an Upper Secondary Qualification" (TUVA) - a one-year, individualised education programme positioned between lower and upper secondary education.

Sweden: Written individual development plans, so-called IUPs, only apply to ISCED 1. Individual study plans for newly arrived students only apply to ISCED 2 (grades 7-9). Individual study plans for all only apply to ISCED 34.

Indicator 3: Teacher competences related to ELET promoted through top-level competence frameworks for ITE and/or top-level CPD programmes, ISCED 1-34, 2024/2025

data.Unnamed: 1: Diagnosing ELET risk factors (e.g. learning difficulties, truancy, illness, peer-influence or teacher-student-relationships)
data.Unnamed: 3: Developing effective interventions to prevent ELET
data.Unnamed: 5: Promoting a positive school climate (e.g. through class management, conflict resolution, relationship building, and bullying and violence prevention)
data.Unnamed: 7: Teaching diverse learners and promoting inclusive approaches (e.g. through avoiding stereotyping, prejudice, and other forms of discrimination)
data.Unnamed: 9: Teaching in multilingual and multicultural settings
data.Unnamed: 11: Awareness of learners' social and emotional development
data.Unnamed: 13: Collaborating effectively with families from different backgrounds
data.Unnamed: 15: Managing their own (i.e. teachers’) well-being, mental health and stress
data.Unnamed: 19: No top-level competence framework for ITE

data.Unnamed: 22: A competence framework can be defined as a set of statements outlining what a teacher should know and be able to do. It typically describes the skills, knowledge, and competences required for effective teaching. The format, value, and recognition of such frameworks can vary between countries.

Competence frameworks may inform the content of initial teacher education (ITE), which is designed to equip prospective teachers with core professional competences and to develop the attitudes essential for their future roles and responsibilities. ITE also  usually includes a first practical teaching experience through in-school placements.

Continuing professional development (CPD) refers to the in-service training that teachers undertake throughout their careers to broaden, deepen, and update their knowledge, skills, and professional attitudes. It can take both formal and non-formal forms and may cover subject-specific content as well as pedagogical approaches.

A wide range of CPD formats is available, including courses, seminars, workshops, degree programmes, peer or self-observation and reflection, mentoring, participation in teacher networks, and observation visits. In some cases, CPD activities may lead to additional qualifications or certifications.
Belgium (BE de): There are no ITE programmes for teachers of secondary schools.

Belgium (BE nl): The category 'Other' refers to the fact that school teams independently tailor their CPD programmes to their learning needs without any mandated requirements from the Flemish government.
Ireland: Data only apply to ISCED 1 and 24.

Luxembourg: While there is no national competence framework for ITE, the Bachelor degree in educational sciences at the University of Luxembourg offers courses covering some of these competencies for future primary school teachers (ISCED 1).
Austria: The category 'Other' refers to some additional competences areas that are being promoted, such as promoting gender equality, inclusive pedagogy or teaching effectiveness.
Romania: The category 'Other' refers to teacher competences in using technology to facilitate the learning process.
Liechtenstein: There is no ITE in Liechtenstein.

Indicator 4: Top-level policies and measures for addressing absenteeism, ISCED 1–34, 2024/2025

data.Unnamed: 8: No top-level policy/measure to address absenteeism

data.Unnamed: 10: Policies and measures to address absenteeism often involve a combination of preventive, supportive, and corrective strategies aimed at enabling timely interventions to reduce student disengagement and prevent early leaving from education and training (ELET). Key measures include:

1. Family and community engagement: Collaborating with families and community organisations to identify and address the underlying causes of absenteeism, such as transportation difficulties, family responsibilities, or lack of academic or emotional support.
2. Supportive interventions: Providing targeted support such as counselling, mentoring, or case management for students with persistent or high levels of absenteeism.

3. Flexible scheduling: Offering flexible timetables or alternative learning arrangements, including online or blended learning, to accommodate students facing barriers related to health, caregiving responsibilities, or other personal circumstances.
4. Improving school climate: Creating a positive and inclusive school environment where students feel safe, supported, respected, and motivated to attend regularly.
5. Policy enforcement: Establishing and clearly communicating attendance policies, while ensuring consistent, fair implementation that balances accountability with appropriate support mechanisms.
6. Health and well-being programmes: Implementing initiatives that promote students’ mental and physical health, which can improve their capacity to engage consistently with school.

Belgium (BE fr): At ISCED 1, school principals can accept unlimited parental excuses for absences due to exceptional circumstances like family issues or health problems, whereas, at ISCED 24-34, such excuses are limited to 8 to 16 half-days annually depending on the school's internal regulations.
Belgium (German-speaking Community): The SKEI project applies to ISCED 1; the Time Out project applies to ISCED 24 and 34.
Estonia: The Health and wellbeing programmes KiVa and Schools in Motion apply tp ISCED 1-24.
Croatia and Slovenia: There are differences in regulations on absences between ISCED 1-24 and ISCED34.
Lithuania: The life skills curriculum only applies to ISCED 1-24.
Luxembourg: Except for the obligation to notify the Ministry after 48h of missed classes, the listed measures do not apply to ISCED 1.
Malta: The category 'Other' refers to blended learning pathways.

Portugal: The category 'Other' refers to a range of other policy initiatives to combat absenteeism, such as inclusive education, targeted programmes like Priority Intervention Educational Territories, alternative secondary education pathways, and distance learning.
Slovakia: The category 'Other' refers to desegregation measures.

Finland: At ISCED 34, the education provider decides on the regulations regarding student absence. The category 'Other' refers to measures to instructions and tools for teachers, principals and managers on how to support school attendance and address absences.

Sweden: Special teaching groups and individual teaching apply only to ISCED levels 1-24. Extended teaching is specific to ISCED 34, while home teaching for illness is available at all levels. Consultation with student health is mandatory in primary education (ISCED 1-2) and recommended for ISCED 3.

Bosnia and Herzegovina: Since primary education is compulsory, unlike secondary education, disciplinary measures differ, with primary students exceeding the absence limit facing transfer to another school rather than expulsion.
Iceland: Policy enforcement and health and well-being programmes only apply to ISCED 1-24.

Montenegro: The category 'Other' refers to the fact that the Montenegrin Educational Information System allows parents to track student achievements, attendance, and disciplinary measures using a code provided by the head teacher at the start of the school year.

Norway: Absence monitoring applies to all ISCED levels, with a 10% absence limit for ISCED 34. From 1 August 2025, students must self-certify absences up to 10%, after which a medical certificate is required. Exemptions for political, religious, and medical reasons remain, absences will appear on school certificates, and principals can allow grading for absences up to 15% in justified cases.

Indicator 5: Top-level policies and measures for monitoring and reaching out to non-enrolled youth, 2024/2025

data.Unnamed: 9: No top-level policy/measure for monitoring and reaching out to non-enrolled youth

data.Unnamed: 11: Policies and measures to monitor and reach out to non-enrolled youth aim to identify, support, and reintegrate out-of-school young people into education and training pathways. Effective strategies typically combine targeted outreach, individual support, community engagement, and systematic monitoring. Key measures include:

1. Community-based outreach: Collaborating with local community organisations, NGOs, social workers, and other stakeholders to identify and engage out-of-school youth, particularly in remote or marginalised areas.
2. Home visits and counselling: Carrying out home visits to understand the reasons for school dropout and to provide personalised support and guidance for re-enrolment.
3. Financial and material support: Removing economic barriers by providing scholarships, school supplies, transportation, and meals to facilitate a return to education.
4. Youth mentorship programmes: Linking out-of-school youth with mentors who can offer guidance on educational pathways, vocational options, and life skills.
5. Youth and community centres: Establishing accessible spaces where young people can receive academic support, career counselling, tutoring, and referral to social services.
6. Awareness campaigns: Raising awareness among families and communities about the value of education and the resources available to support re-enrolment.
7. Regular monitoring and reporting: Defining clear benchmarks and implementing consistent data collection and reporting mechanisms to assess progress and refine outreach strategies.

Czechia: The category 'Other' refers to regular assessments of the child's and family's situation, the preparation of an individual child protection plan, and the organisation of case conferences, as mandated by the Act on Social and Legal Protection of Children.
Germany: The category 'Other' refers to Training guarantee and youth employment agencies.

Denmark: The category 'Other' refers to the municipal Kommunale Ungeindsats (KUI), responsible for supporting and guiding young people under 25 who have not completed secondary education or started in a full time job.
Netherlands: The category 'Other' refers to money at the disposal of schools and municipalities to address the needs of non-enrolled youth.
Finland: The category 'Other' refers to workshop activities.
Montenegro: The category 'Other' refers to the Employment Agency of Montenegro (EAM) services for all unemployed persons and other job seekers, including those who have dropped out of education.
Norway: The category 'Other' refers to the county authority's obligation to provide follow-up services for young people who are entitled to education and training.

Serbia: The category 'Other' refers to measures such as integrating financial or material assistance, or youth mentorship programmes, with awareness campaigns, typically implemented as project-oriented efforts at the local or district level rather than as top-level policies.

columns: System-level indicators for monitoring education and training systems in Europe – 2025

data.Unnamed: 1: There is collaboration with municipalities, especially in Brussels, involving local prevention units and partnerships with the non-profit organisation Foyer, which serves Roma and Travelers.

Since 2018, a data linkage has been in place between Education and the VDAB database to better map these young people. As a result, the Flemish government can identify early school leavers who are neither pursuing education, training, or other forms of education, nor employed.

Schooling is mandatory until age 16, but students have the right to continue their education afterward. Free transportation is offered to all students who travel to schools outside their residential area, including those over 16 who choose to continue their studies. Additionally, free textbooks are available for students from 1st to 12th grade. Students over 16 who continue studying can receive social benefits until age 20. Youth mentorship programmes and access to youth and community centers are also available for students over 16 who remain in education through 12th grade.

The framework for addressing non-enrolled youth ensures social inclusion and educational continuity for individuals up to 18 years. It involves collaboration with local authorities and non-profits, addressing absenteeism issues. Students receive free transportation, textbooks, and social benefits to support education beyond compulsory schooling. Guided by the Social and Legal Protection of Children Act, it includes youth mentorship, community centre involvement, and home visits. Municipal authorities conduct field social work and outreach with at-risk families. Awareness campaigns funded by the Ministry of Education highlight the importance of education and preventing risky behaviour. Trained social workers monitor progress to align measures with individual needs, following guidelines like the Methodological Recommendation on Social Work with Families at Risk.

The Kommunale Ungeindsats (KUI) is a municipal initiative dedicated to supporting individuals under 25 who have completed primary education but have not yet pursued secondary education or secured full-time employment (at least 20 hours per week). KUI's primary objective is to guide these young people towards further education or work opportunities. To achieve this, KUI collaborates with the individual to develop an education plan that coordinates resources and initiatives from the education, employment, and social units within the municipality, aiming to facilitate their transition into secondary education or employment.

Community-based youth outreach includes several initiatives to aid young people's transition from school to work. Outreach youth social work targets those avoiding traditional services, offering professional guidance in public spaces. The JOBLINGE programme collaborates with businesses and government to combat youth unemployment through mentorship and vocational training. The Federal Employment Agency supports career orientation with online and personal counselling. Comprehensive support involves early preventative services, awareness campaigns with information about training programmes and jobs, customised funding, and a training guarantee that includes internships and mobility grants. Youth employment agencies promote cooperation among agencies for streamlined support. Additionally, the ESF Plus Programme "JUGEND STÄRKEN: Brücken in die Eigenständigkeit" supports young adults aged 14 to 26 with socio-educational resources to manage independent living aspects like housing and education.

The National Programme of Support Measures for NEETs (2023–2029) facilitates mobile youth work and youth centres to aid NEETs with basic or lower education in continuing their studies. The Youth Guarantee Support System targets individuals aged 16–29, assisting in their re-entry into education or the labour market. The proportion of NEETs is consistently monitored through the Estonian Education Information System, as well as the data from the Social Insurance Board, the Unemployment Insurance Fund, and the Employment Register.

The regulatory framework for protecting minors in Spain, established by the Organic Law 1/1996 and Law 26/2015, supports various regional initiatives aimed at education and social integration. Community-based outreach programmes, supported by grants from the Ministry of Education, help combat educational inequalities, monitor school absenteeism, and provide socio-educational activities. Home visits and counselling are part of regional plans to address absenteeism, as seen in Aragón. Financial and material assistance, including scholarships like Andalucía's Beca 6000 and Second Chance Scholarship, support students over 16 to prevent dropout and encourage continued education. Youth mentorship programmes, such as those in Castilla-La Mancha and Valencia, pair mentors with students to enhance academic and personal development, while youth and community centres offer diverse activities for ages 14-30. Awareness campaigns, as defined in the País Vasco, aim to inform and engage society in supporting education and youth development, forming a comprehensive approach to addressing the needs of young people.

Community-based outreach for adolescents and young adults includes programmes like FOQUALE (i.e. Training-Qualification-Employment Networks), which coordinate school and partner efforts to provide personalised paths back to education or work. The Mission de lutte contre le décrochage scolaire (MLDS) and "Return to School Structures" support the reintegration of school dropouts, while the Campus des métiers et des qualifications (CMQ) enhances vocational training opportunities. "Missions locales" facilitate home visits and counselling to address dropouts' needs and ease re-enrollment. Financial assistance, such as mobility aid and the youth commitment contract (CEJ), helps overcome economic barriers to education. Youth mentorship programmes under "1 jeune / 1 solution" offer individualised support, with the "1 jeune - 1 mentor" plan launched in 2021 to boost youth autonomy. Awareness campaigns within this framework highlight training opportunities for school dropouts. Regular monitoring and reporting, through the interministerial information exchange system (SIEI) and drop-out follow-up and support platforms (PSAD), ensure comprehensive identification and intervention for youth dropping out of school.

The National Youth Programme for 2023 to 2025 aims to enhance local and regional youth policies by providing financial grants to develop respective youth programmes. These projects will actively involve young people, especially those with fewer opportunities, in designing relevant measures and activities. The activities will also engage out-of-school youth.

The orientation reform, Mission 4-C1, introduces orientation modules in secondary schools and a digital platform to link education, universities, and the labour market, helping students make informed choices and reducing dropout and NEET rates. These modules personalise and broaden study plans, integrating hands-on learning and extracurricular activities to explore students' skills and interests. Guidelines from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) aim to connect education cycles, support thoughtful choices, and reduce dropouts, enabling access to tertiary education. Collaborations with local communities, educational institutions, and the labour market support this networked process. Secondary schools offer 30-hour orientation modules yearly, documented in E-Portfolios and supported by digital platforms for teachers and families. The PNRR funds 15-hour orientation courses in upper secondary schools through university partnerships. Supported by the UNICA platform and national assessment by INVALSI, these initiatives align with the NEET Plan's phased approach to tackle youth inactivity, involving the Youth Guarantee, Youth Desks at Employment Centres, and the Universal Civil Service.

Second chance evening schools are offered for citizens aged 19 and above, free of tuition or expenses. The Ministry of Labor maintains records of youth over 19 who have not completed upper secondary education. To support these individuals, the educational counseling services at the Ministry of Education work collaboratively with the Ministry of Labor to encourage enrollment in evening schools. This collaboration is legally supported; the Council of Ministers established the National Body for Lifelong Guidance in 2009, chaired by the Ministers of Education, Sports and Youth, and Labor and Social Insurance, to address the educational needs of these young citizens.

The Youth International Programmes Agency leverages EU and municipal support to offer young people numerous project opportunities. It provides guidance on drafting projects, shares valuable information about European opportunities, and fosters experience exchanges. The Agency manages several EU programmes, such as "Erasmus+" for youth, the "European Solidarity Corps," and oversees the European Commission's youth information network "Eurodesk." It also supports "eTwinning," the national Youth Policy Programme, and projects like "Development of the Digital Youth Work System in Local Governments" and "NAMELY and DO 2.0." Continuing from previous EU funding periods, the "NAMELY and DO 2.0 for NEET Youth" project aims to enhance skills for individuals aged 15-29 who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET), encouraging their participation in educational and vocational activities, employment opportunities, or involvement with NGOs and youth centres.

The community-based outreach includes the Multidimensional Family Therapy Programme, targeting behavioral issues in 11-17-year-olds to help reintegrate them into education and social norms. Home visits and counseling through case management provide comprehensive support to prevent rights violations. Preventive services, such as social skills development and family conferences, aim to strengthen family dynamics. "Jungtys," a mentorship programme for 14-29-year-olds from 2024-2028, focuses on reducing youth inactivity by facilitating reentry into the labour market or education through personalised plans. Financial and material assistance ensures school transportation and covers costs for supplies and meals under the Law on Education and under the Law on Social Support for Students. Youth and community centers offer day social care to develop life skills. The Student Register and NEMIS system track uneducated children and dropouts to address their return to education.

The National Youth Service (SNJ) proactively monitors and engages school dropouts to encourage their reintegration into education or the workforce. By leveraging monthly dropout lists, agents reach out to young individuals for initial interviews, employing diverse communication methods if initial contact is unresponsive. SNJ offers tailored support and a variety of flexible, practical programmes, such as voluntary services, workshops, internships, orientation classes, and training, to help young people aged 16 to 30 gain experience and skills. The workshops, spread across three sites, attract a diverse group, including international protection beneficiaries, and focus on creative skills, such as woodworking and sewing. The SNJ also coordinates annual events like the "Deng Zukunft, Däi Wee" fair and the Engagement Evening, which connect youth with career opportunities and recognise their efforts in transition projects. A Dropout Report, developed in collaboration with the Ministry of National Education, provides systematic data analysis to effectively monitor and address dropout rates.

Community-based outreach and youth and community centres are facilitated by Agenzija Zghazagh, a government agency focused on youth outreach and inclusion. While their services extend beyond just supporting unenrolled youth, they play a crucial role in youth development. Youth Cafes provide safe, alternative leisure spaces for individuals aged 13 to 25 to interact with peers, explore talents, and enhance personal and social skills. Youth Hubs offer a recreational setting where youth workers collaborate with young people on projects and initiatives to unlock their potential. Detached Youth Work involves youth workers engaging with young people in discussions and informing them about various opportunities and issues.

Together with schools and municipalities, the government is implementing measures to encourage students to return to education. As a result of the decentralized system,  top-level authorities primarily provide the financial backing, while the execution of most actions is carried out by schools and municipalities.

The Compulsory Training Act (Ausbildungspflichtgesetz), introduced in 2016, mandates that all young people under 18 who have completed compulsory schooling and are permanently resident in Austria must continue with education or training. This obligation remains in effect until they reach 18 or successfully complete additional education or training. To ensure compliance, young people under 18 are monitored for enrollment in education or apprenticeship programmes. Youth Coaching is a supportive counselling programme designed for those finishing mandatory schooling or who have dropped out, offering personalised assistance to help them re-enter the educational system or secure an apprenticeship. Youth coaches also provide counselling for those who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET).

The Youth Employment Initiative (YEI), part of Poland’s Knowledge Education Development Programme, was funded by the European Social Fund (ESF), the Youth Employment Initiative (YEI) budget, and the state budget, with over EUR 5.4 billion allocated, including more than EUR 2 billion specifically for youth support. It aims to activate unemployed young people under 30 through vocational guidance, training, internships, apprenticeships, subsidised employment, business grants, and mobility support. Targeting regions with youth unemployment above 25%, support was extended nationwide to include those aged 15-29, particularly NEETs (Not in Employment, Education, or Training), benefiting around 700,000 young people. Additionally, the 2023-2024 “Time for the Young” pilot programme, backed by PLN 60 million from the Labour Fund, established 76 advisory centres offering vocational, psychological, educational, financial, and housing support. Implemented by the Ministry of Labour, Family and Social Policy, the initiative involved collaboration between labour offices, training institutions, NGOs, and social services to enhance youth employment and social inclusion.

The annual national report on education, chapters 1 and 5 cover the essential statistical indicators for national monitoring and reporting the rate of enrolled vs. not enrolled students for all levels of education.  This form of monitoring and reporting is constant and consistent from year to year and it supports the initiatives for reaching out the non-enrolled youth through targeted initiatives like research-based surveys, studies and support inititiatives.

PUM-o+ is a dynamic, project-based programme designed for young adults (ages 15-26) who have dropped out or failed to complete basic, lower, or upper secondary education. It also supports students at risk of dropping out and younger participants in the Adult Basic School programme. This initiative empowers vulnerable young people by helping them re-enter education or the job market, discover their talents, develop essential skills, and break free from the cycle of failure. The programme is implemented by the Ministry of Labour, Family, Social Affairs and Equal Opportunities, in collaboration with the Employment Service of the Republic of Slovenia and other external partners. It is co-financed by the European Social Fund as part of the European Cohesion Policy Programme 2021-2027.

Outreach youth work provides safe and confidential support for young people under 29, helping them access essential services, education, and employment opportunities. It is voluntary and focuses on empowerment, independence, and social participation. The Regional State Administrative Agency allocates over €50 million annually for youth-related initiatives, including One-Stop Guidance Centers, which offer free assistance on various life matters for those under 30. Workshop activities foster inclusion, skill development, and career readiness through multidisciplinary collaboration. Additionally, Save the Children Finland’s mentoring programme supports middle school students in their studies, fostering motivation, confidence, and learning success. The National Audit Office (VTV) has made efforts to identify, support, and reintegrate young people disengaged from work and education. Its January 2025 report reveals that 9% of 15–29-year-olds have been neither working nor studying in recent years, and in 2023, one in five 20–24-year-olds had only completed comprehensive school.

Municipalities are responsible for identifying relevant local and civil society actors—such as schools, social services, and employment agencies—for collaboration in supporting young people. This cooperation should be outlined in an action plan with measurable goals and expected outcomes. Through  the municipal activity responsibility (KAA), municipalities must monitor and offer tailored support to individuals under 20 who are not in upper secondary education. These efforts, aimed at motivating youth to start or resume education, must be continuous, documented, and tracked in a municipal register.

As part of the government's action plan to reduce youth violence, a study and career counselor has been appointed to support and engage children who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET). Youth and community centers remain open to all children, with a particular focus on vulnerable groups. Additionally, the government has partially funded a traveling youth center aimed at reaching 12–16-year-olds who do not participate in extracurricular activities, exhibit negative communication patterns, engage in risky behavior, or face social challenges.

The Law on Vocational Education allows students who have started but not completed their education to continue as part-time students. These students attend preparatory (instructional-consultative) classes and take exams to progress in their studies. Schools provide guidance on education pathways and organize structured support to help students develop essential skills and successfully complete their education.

The county authority is required to provide follow-up services for young people who are entitled to education and training under Section 5-1 of the Education Act (upper secondary education) and who are neither enrolled in education nor employed, as outlined in Section 9-4 of the Education Act. These services must be available until the end of the year in which the individual turns 24.

Targeted measures for Roma students, who are the majority of non-enrolled youth, focus on increasing primary school enrollment to 90% and secondary school completion to 50% by 2030. These efforts include community outreach in collaboration with local authorities and ministries, as well as enforcing regulations to prevent the wrongful placement of Roma students in special education. Progress includes a rise in secondary school enrollment from 22% in 2014 to 28% in 2019, with an 85.4% primary school enrollment rate and a 7% reduction in dropout rates.

National policy outlines provisions for young people above the compulsory school age who require guidance to complete their education. It emphasises providing personalised support to help these individuals finish their schooling, with the aim of ensuring they have the necessary resources, advice, and opportunities. The guidance process includes regular monitoring and tailored educational pathways to encourage completion and facilitate further career or academic goals.
